contribution: Opens chapter 3 as a historical investigation: why chemical burning and gravitational contraction (Helmholtz, Kelvin) failed to explain the Sun's energy, how Eddington in 1920 used Aston's mass measurement to propose hydrogen fusion, and a conceptual estimate of the Sun's lifetime from $E = \Delta m \cdot c^2$ with clearly stated assumptions.
learn: compare chemical, gravitational and nuclear explanations of the Sun's energy.
calculate how long an energy source lasts with $t = E/L$.
evaluate a lifetime estimate by its simplifying assumptions.
prior: A nucleus has less mass than its free nucleons, and $E = \Delta m \cdot c^2$ gives the energy (chapter *Mass defect and binding energy*)
Power is energy per time, $P = E/t$ (earlier physics courses)

activities.text: Every second, the Sun sends $3.83 \cdot 10^{26}\ \text{J}$ of energy into space, more than humankind uses in half a million years. Rocks on Earth contain fossils of living things that needed sunlight hundreds of millions of years ago, and the oldest rocks and meteorites are billions of years old. Around 1860, the best physicists in the world could not explain how any fuel could last that long.
activities.question: What could keep the Sun shining for billions of years?

activities.title: Review: mass and energy
activities.prompt: In the chapter *Mass defect and binding energy*, a helium-4 nucleus turned out to have less mass than its free nucleons. What does this mean?

choices.text: Energy was released when the nucleus formed.
choices.feedback: Right: the missing mass left as energy, $E = \Delta m \cdot c^2$. Today you see why this solved one of the great puzzles of the 19th century.

choices.text: Some nucleons were lost when the nucleus formed.
choices.feedback: No nucleon is lost: helium-4 has $4$ nucleons, like its parts. The bound system has less *energy*, and so less mass.

choices.text: The measurement must be wrong, since mass is conserved.
choices.feedback: The measurements are very precise. Mass alone is not conserved in nuclear reactions; mass and energy together are.

activities.title: Prediction 1: a Sun made of coal
activities.prompt: Imagine that the whole Sun were coal, burning with plenty of oxygen and giving off today's power. Roughly how long could it shine?

choices.text: A few thousand years
choices.feedback: Right: about $5000$ years. Even the most generous chemical fuel gives only some $10^{7}\ \text{J}$ per kilogram, and the Sun uses energy at an enormous rate.

choices.text: A few million years
choices.feedback: The calculation gives only about $5000$ years: $M \cdot 32.5\ \text{MJ/kg} : L \approx 1.7 \cdot 10^{11}\ \text{s}$. The Sun is so powerful that even its huge mass of coal would burn quickly.

choices.text: A few billion years
choices.feedback: That is the real age of the Sun, but no chemical fuel gets near it: a Sun of coal would last about $5000$ years. This is why chemical energy was rejected.

activities.title: Prediction 2: the best explanation
activities.prompt: Which of these explanations could keep the Sun shining for billions of years?

choices.text: Slow shrinking, which turns gravitational energy into heat.
choices.feedback: Contraction gives more than burning, but only a few tens of millions of years: Kelvin's own limit was about $20$ million years.

choices.text: Heat stored inside the Sun since it formed, slowly cooling.
choices.feedback: A cooling body without a source would fade even faster than a contracting one. Something must keep producing energy.

choices.text: Turning a small part of its mass into energy in nuclei.
choices.feedback: Right. Fusing hydrogen into helium turns $0.71\ \%$ of the fused mass into energy, enough for about $10^{10}$ years.

choices.text: Chemical burning of the Sun's hydrogen with its oxygen.
choices.feedback: Chemical reactions release only a few electronvolts per molecule; a Sun of fuel would last only thousands of years.

activities.title: Investigation 1: test the chemical explanation
activities.source_note: The Sun's mass and luminosity: IAU 2015 nominal values as given in Wikipedia, Sun; heat of combustion of anthracite coal: Wikipedia, Heat of combustion (both checked 1 November 2026).
activities.text:
Test prediction 1 with real values. The coal is the best case: anthracite, and the oxygen it needs is not counted.

| Quantity | Value |
| --- | --- |
| mass of the Sun $M$ | $1.99 \cdot 10^{30}\ \text{kg}$ |
| luminosity of the Sun $L$ | $3.83 \cdot 10^{26}\ \text{W}$ |
| heat of combustion of anthracite $q$ | $32.5\ \text{MJ/kg}$ |
| one year | $3.156 \cdot 10^{7}\ \text{s}$ |

question.prompt: Calculate how many years a Sun made of anthracite could shine at the power $L$. Use $E = qM$ and $t = E/L$.
hints: First the energy: $E = qM$, with $q$ in $\text{J/kg}$.
$t = E/L$ gives seconds; divide by $3.156 \cdot 10^{7}\ \text{s}$ per year.

mistakes.feedback: This is the time in seconds. Divide by $3.156 \cdot 10^{7}\ \text{s}$ to get years.

question.solution:
**Given:** $M = 1.99 \cdot 10^{30}\ \text{kg}$, $L = 3.83 \cdot 10^{26}\ \text{W}$, $q = 32.5\ \text{MJ/kg}$

**Find:** the time $t$ in years

**Principle:** Burning releases the heat of combustion for every kilogram of fuel. At a constant power, the time is the energy divided by the power.

**Formula:**

$$t = \frac{E}{L} = \frac{qM}{L}$$

**Unit conversions:** $q = 32.5\ \text{MJ/kg} = 3.25 \cdot 10^{7}\ \text{J/kg}$; $1\ \text{W} = 1\ \text{J/s}$; $1\ \text{a} = 3.156 \cdot 10^{7}\ \text{s}$

**Substitution:**

$$\begin{aligned} t &= \frac{3.25 \cdot 10^{7}\ \text{J/kg} \cdot 1.99 \cdot 10^{30}\ \text{kg}}{3.83 \cdot 10^{26}\ \text{J/s}} \\ &= 1.69 \cdot 10^{11}\ \text{s} \\ &= \frac{1.69 \cdot 10^{11}\ \text{s}}{3.156 \cdot 10^{7}\ \text{s/a}} = 5350\ \text{a} \end{aligned}$$

**Answer:** about $5000$ years ($5350$ years with these values). One significant figure is enough for an argument about orders of magnitude.

**Reasonableness:** Human history is longer than this, and fossils are millions of times older. Even a perfect chemical fuel cannot explain the Sun.

activities.title: Investigation 2: read the historical source
activities.text:
Arthur Eddington, *The Internal Constitution of the Stars*, address to the British Association, Cardiff, 24 August 1920 (printed in *Nature* 106, 1920). Short extracts:

> "A star is drawing on some vast reservoir of energy by means unknown to us. This reservoir can scarcely be other than the sub-atomic energy which, it is known, exists abundantly in all matter."

> "[...] Aston has further shown conclusively that the mass of the helium atom is less than the sum of the masses of the 4 hydrogen atoms which enter into it."

> "There is a loss of mass in the synthesis amounting to about 1 part in 120, the atomic weight of hydrogen being 1.008 and that of helium just 4."

The word *synthesis* means building something from parts.

question.prompt: What kind of evidence did Eddington use for his idea?

choices.text: A laboratory measurement of the masses of atoms
choices.feedback: Right: Aston's mass spectrograph showed that helium is lighter than four hydrogen atoms. Eddington connected this measurement with $E = mc^2$ and with the Sun's power.

choices.text: An experiment that fused hydrogen in a laboratory
choices.feedback: Nobody had fused hydrogen in 1920. The first laboratory fusion reactions came in 1934, and they used deuterium. Eddington's evidence was a measurement of masses.

choices.text: Signals of nuclear reactions seen in sunlight
choices.feedback: Sunlight comes from the surface and shows nothing of the core's reactions. Eddington argued from Aston's measurement of atomic masses.

activities.title: Investigation 3: the story in order

activities.text:
Word bank

luminosity · energy source · chemical energy · gravitational contraction · radioactivity · sub-atomic energy · evidence · estimate · assumption · to last · to run out · to contradict · a conflict between

Sentence starters

  • Kelvin's estimate contradicted …
  • The evidence from geology suggests that …
  • One possible explanation is …
  • Kelvin could not have known that …
  • I think the geologists / Kelvin were right, because …

activities.title: Discussion: Kelvin against the geologists
activities.prompt: Discuss with a partner, then write four or five sentences of your own. In the 1860s–1890s, Kelvin said that the Sun was at most a few tens of millions of years old, while geologists and biologists needed hundreds of millions. Who was right, and why? What did Kelvin not know? What does this story tell you about how science deals with a conflict between two kinds of evidence?
activities.model: The geologists and biologists were right about the time: the Earth and the Sun are about $4.6$ billion years old. Kelvin's estimate contradicted the evidence from rocks and fossils, but his physics was correct for the energy sources he knew, chemical burning and contraction. Kelvin could not have known about nuclear energy, which was discovered only after radioactivity in 1896. The conflict was a sign that a piece of physics was missing. One lesson is that when careful evidence from two fields disagrees, the disagreement itself can point to new science.
criteria: The answer says that the long timescale of geology and biology was right (billions of years).
The answer says that Kelvin's calculation was based on the energy sources known at the time.
The answer names the missing piece: energy in atomic nuclei (radioactivity, fusion).
The answer draws a conclusion about evidence or the way science works, with a sentence starter.

activities.title: Words of the lesson
Back to your predictions
activities.prompt: Compare your predictions with your calculation, the source and the theory. Then answer the opening question in one or two sentences: why hasn't the Sun burned out?

activities.title: How fast does the Sun lose mass?
activities.prompt: The Sun radiates $L = 3.83 \cdot 10^{26}\ \text{W}$. How much mass does it turn into energy every second? Use $c = 3.00 \cdot 10^{8}\ \text{m/s}$ and give the answer in kilograms.
hints: In one second the Sun gives away the energy $E = 3.83 \cdot 10^{26}\ \text{J}$.

mistakes.feedback: This is the mass of hydrogen *fused* per second. Only $0.71\ \%$ of it turns into energy; the question asks for that part, $\Delta m = E/c^2$.

activities.solution:
**Given:** $L = 3.83 \cdot 10^{26}\ \text{W}$, $t = 1\ \text{s}$, $c = 3.00 \cdot 10^{8}\ \text{m/s}$

**Find:** the mass $\Delta m$ that becomes energy in one second

**Principle:** Mass–energy equivalence: the radiated energy corresponds to a lost mass $\Delta m = E/c^2$; in one second the energy is $E = Lt$.

**Formula:**

$$\Delta m = \frac{E}{c^2} = \frac{Lt}{c^2}$$

**Unit conversions:** $1\ \text{W} \cdot 1\ \text{s} = 1\ \text{J}$, and $1\ \text{J} = 1\ \text{kg} \cdot \text{m}^2/\text{s}^2$, so the result is in kilograms.

**Substitution:**

$$\begin{aligned} \Delta m &= \frac{3.83 \cdot 10^{26}\ \text{J/s} \cdot 1\ \text{s}}{(3.00 \cdot 10^{8}\ \text{m/s})^2} \\ &= 4.26 \cdot 10^{9}\ \text{kg} \end{aligned}$$

**Answer:** $\Delta m \approx 4.26 \cdot 10^{9}\ \text{kg}$, about $4$ million tonnes every second, three significant figures as in $L$.

**Reasonableness:** It sounds huge, but over the Sun's whole age of $4.6$ billion years ($1.45 \cdot 10^{17}\ \text{s}$) it adds up to $6 \cdot 10^{26}\ \text{kg}$, only about $0.03\ \%$ of the Sun's mass.

activities.title: Kelvin's estimate
activities.prompt: If the Sun formed by contraction from a huge cloud, it has released about $E = GM^2/R$ of gravitational energy (an order-of-magnitude estimate). Calculate how many years this energy lasts at today's power. Use $G = 6.674 \cdot 10^{-11}\ \text{N} \cdot \text{m}^2/\text{kg}^2$, $M = 1.99 \cdot 10^{30}\ \text{kg}$, $R = 6.96 \cdot 10^{8}\ \text{m}$ and $L = 3.83 \cdot 10^{26}\ \text{W}$.
hints: Divide the seconds by $3.156 \cdot 10^{7}\ \text{s}$ per year.

mistakes.feedback: This is the time in seconds; divide by $3.156 \cdot 10^{7}\ \text{s}$ per year.

activities.solution:
**Given:** $G = 6.674 \cdot 10^{-11}\ \text{N} \cdot \text{m}^2/\text{kg}^2$, $M = 1.99 \cdot 10^{30}\ \text{kg}$, $R = 6.96 \cdot 10^{8}\ \text{m}$, $L = 3.83 \cdot 10^{26}\ \text{W}$

**Find:** the time $t$ in years

**Principle:** When a cloud contracts into a star, its gravitational potential energy decreases by about $GM^2/R$, and this energy is radiated. At a constant power, $t = E/L$.

**Formula:**

$$t = \frac{GM^2}{RL}$$

**Unit conversions:** $1\ \text{N} \cdot \text{m} = 1\ \text{J}$ and $1\ \text{W} = 1\ \text{J/s}$; $1\ \text{a} = 3.156 \cdot 10^{7}\ \text{s}$.

**Substitution:**

$$\begin{aligned} t &= \frac{6.674 \cdot 10^{-11} \cdot (1.99 \cdot 10^{30})^2}{6.96 \cdot 10^{8} \cdot 3.83 \cdot 10^{26}}\ \text{s} \\ &= 9.91 \cdot 10^{14}\ \text{s} = 3.14 \cdot 10^{7}\ \text{a} \end{aligned}$$

**Answer:** about $3 \cdot 10^{7}$ years, $30$ million years; one significant figure, because $GM^2/R$ is only an order-of-magnitude estimate.

**Reasonableness:** This agrees in order of magnitude with Kelvin's limit of about $20$ million years, and it is $150$ times shorter than the real age of the Sun.

activities.title: Find the error
activities.prompt: A student estimates the Sun's lifetime as $t = \frac{Mc^2}{L}$ and gets $1.5 \cdot 10^{13}$ years, a thousand times the age of the Universe. What is wrong?

choices.text: Fusion turns only about $0.7\ \%$ of the fused mass into energy.
choices.feedback: Right. $Mc^2$ would mean that all of the Sun's mass disappears. Hydrogen becomes helium, and only $0.71\ \%$ of the fused mass, in the core only, becomes energy.

choices.text: The formula should use $c$, not $c^2$.
choices.feedback: $E = \Delta m \cdot c^2$ is right. The error is the mass: not all of $M$ turns into energy.

choices.text: The Sun's power was much higher in the past.
choices.feedback: The young Sun was in fact a little *less* bright. The real error is that $Mc^2$ treats the whole mass as fuel.

activities.title: 1. Concept: why not chemistry?
activities.prompt: Why can chemical burning not explain the Sun's energy?

choices.text: Chemical reactions release far too little energy per kilogram.
choices.feedback: Right: some $10^{7}\ \text{J/kg}$, so even a Sun of coal would last only about $5000$ years.

choices.text: There is no oxygen in the Sun, so nothing can burn.
choices.feedback: Even with free oxygen, the best fuel would last only thousands of years. The problem is the energy per kilogram, not the oxygen.

choices.text: The Sun is too hot for chemical reactions to start.
choices.feedback: Heat does not stop the argument: the decisive point is that burning gives too little energy per kilogram, whatever the temperature.

activities.title: 2. Calculation: the mass lost so far
activities.prompt: The Sun turns about $4.3 \cdot 10^{9}\ \text{kg}$ of mass into energy every second. Its age is $1.45 \cdot 10^{17}\ \text{s}$ and its mass $2.0 \cdot 10^{30}\ \text{kg}$. What part of its mass has it lost so far, assuming a constant rate?

choices.text: about $3\ \%$
choices.feedback: Check the powers of ten: $6.2 \cdot 10^{26} : 2.0 \cdot 10^{30} = 3 \cdot 10^{-4}$, which is $0.03\ \%$, not $3\ \%$.

choices.text: about $30\ \%$
choices.feedback: This would mean that the Sun is a third lighter than when it formed. The lost mass is $6.2 \cdot 10^{26}\ \text{kg}$, only $0.03\ \%$ of $2.0 \cdot 10^{30}\ \text{kg}$.
$0.7\ \%$ is the part of the *fused* hydrogen that becomes energy, not the part of the whole Sun lost so far. Calculate $\Delta m = 4.3 \cdot 10^{9}\ \text{kg/s} \cdot t$.

activities.title: 3. Assumptions: the lifetime estimate
activities.prompt: Our estimate of $10^{10}$ years assumed that $10\ \%$ of the Sun's mass is fused. If $20\ \%$ could be fused, at the same power, what would the estimate be?

choices.text: $2 \cdot 10^{10}$ years
choices.feedback: Right: the energy $E$ is proportional to the fused mass, and $t = E/L$, so twice the fuel lasts twice as long.

choices.text: $5 \cdot 10^{9}$ years
choices.feedback: More fuel at the same power lasts *longer*, not shorter: $t = E/L$ grows with $E$.

choices.text: $10^{10}$ years still
choices.feedback: The fused mass is in the energy: $E = 0.0071 \cdot m_\text{H} \cdot c^2$. Twice the mass gives twice the energy and twice the time.

activities.title: 4. Explain to a younger student
activities.prompt:
A younger student says: "The Sun is a huge fire, and one day it will run out of wood." Write a short, friendly answer (four or five sentences) that corrects the idea with the physics of this lesson. Use at least one number.

Sentence starters

  • It is a good question, but the Sun is not …
  • If the Sun were a fire, it would last only …
  • Instead, in the Sun's core …
  • This is why the Sun can shine for …
activities.model: It is a good question, but the Sun is not a fire. If it were burning like coal, it would have burned out after only about $5000$ years. Instead, in the Sun's core, hydrogen nuclei fuse into helium. A helium nucleus has about $0.7\ \%$ less mass than the four hydrogen atoms it is made from, and that mass becomes energy by $E = mc^2$. This is why the Sun can shine for about $10$ billion years, and it is only about halfway through.
criteria: The answer says that the Sun is not burning (no chemical fire) and gives the short chemical lifetime.
The answer explains fusion of hydrogen into helium and the loss of mass ($E = mc^2$).
The answer gives the lifetime of about $10$ billion years or the age of $4.6$ billion years.
The language is clear and friendly, with full sentences.

activities.text:
Le coin français

In French, the Sun is le Soleil and a star is une étoile. ITER, in the south of France, tries to do on Earth what le Soleil does with l'hydrogène. Listen, repeat, and say the last sentence to your partner.
